Predictive distributions from a fitted illume model

Source: R/ilm_predict.R, R/zzz-iml-aliases.R
ilm_predict.Rd

The engine every other prediction in limn goes through. For each row of newdata it returns the distribution of the predicted quantity: the mean, a new observation, or the linear predictor. That distribution carries the fit's own uncertainty, drawn jointly from the Laplace approximation that gives the fit its standard errors.

Usage

ilm_predict(
  fit,
  newdata,
  target = c("mean", "response", "link"),
  groups,
  uncertainty = c("joint", "fixed", "latent", "none"),
  set = NULL,
  nsim = 1000L,
  seed = 1L,
  time = NULL,
  group = NULL
)

Arguments

fit

A fitted "ilm_model".

newdata

A data frame of rows to predict. Or a named list of data frames, one per scenario, stacked with a .scenario column. A .draw column gives covariates as draws; see Covariates given as draws.

target

"mean", the expected response; "response", a new observation; or "link", the linear predictor.

groups

How the random effects enter; see How the random effects enter. Required when the model has random-effect or correlation-over-time terms.

uncertainty

"joint", "fixed", "latent" or "none"; see Uncertainty.

set

A named list of values to give every row, such as list(dose = c(0, 10)). Each row is repeated once per combination.

nsim

Number of parameter draws.

seed

Seed for the draws. The caller's random-number state is restored afterwards.

time, group

The names of the columns of newdata holding time and the series, such as time = "week", group = "region"; see Time and series columns. Needed only where neither the model nor the rows say.

Value

A predictive distribution, class "ilm_pred": see The prediction object. summary() and as.data.frame() give point estimates and intervals.

  • For "mean" and "link", the point estimate is the value at the estimates, the number predict() gives.

  • For "response", it is the predictive median, with the mean beside it.

How the random effects enter (groups)

A mixed model predicts different things for the same row, depending on the question asked. So groups has no default for a model with random effects or a correlation over time; it must be named. The choices:

  • "fitted": the unit the row names, with that unit's own estimated effects. A level the fit has not seen is predicted as a new unit, and marked in the new_level column.

  • "new": a new, unseen unit. Its effects are drawn from the fitted distribution of effects, afresh in every parameter draw. Rows naming the same unit share its effects within a draw.

  • "typical": a typical unit, with its effects at zero. For a nonlinear link this is not the average unit.

  • "population": the average over units. For target = "mean", the mean is averaged over the distribution of effects, as illume's predict(groups = "population") does. For a new observation, a randomly chosen unit's outcome is the same thing as a new unit's, so it equals "new".

Give one choice for every term, or a list per term, as in list(site = "fitted", ar = "new"). The correlation over time is the term "ar". Smooth terms are part of the mean structure and always enter as fitted.

Over time

With a correlation over time (ilm_ar1(), ilm_car1() or ilm_rw1()), a seen series under "fitted" is continued from its fitted cells:

  • after its last cell, a forecast carried forward from that cell;

  • between two cells, drawn from the bridge between them;

  • before its first cell, carried backward from it.

A new series, or any series under "new", is a fresh path. AR(1) and CAR(1) paths start from their stationary distribution, and a random walk starts from zero at the series' first time. Each series' new times are drawn in sequence, each given the one before, so a draw is one path through them, and rows naming the same series and time share one value, across scenarios too. The model's own parameters are used throughout; nothing is refitted.

For a mean or the linear predictor, the estimate at a seen series' new time is the point forecast: the fitted cells carried forward with no new shocks, at the estimates, as a Kalman filter's point forecast is. For a new series, as for a new unit, it is the predictive median. as.data.frame() gives the expected value beside it, as mean; for counts it can be well above the estimate at long horizons (see as.data.frame.ilm_pred()).

Time and series columns

A prediction records which of its columns hold time and the series, for the trend check (see Checks) and for scaled errors read from the history (ilm_scores()'s history =). It takes them from, in turn:

  • a correlation over time built by name, such as ilm_ar1(~ week | region): its own columns. Naming a different column in time or group is an error, since the model can use only its own, and so are rows from ilm_future() built around a different column that leave the model's own missing;

  • time and group, which name columns of newdata;

  • the rows ilm_future() built, which record their columns.

A model with time only in its formula, such as a trend, a smooth of time or a random slope in time, has no correlation over time to say. Rows from ilm_future() say for it; rows made otherwise, or changed by merge() or subset(), which drop what ilm_future() recorded, need time and group. A correlation over time built from vectors has no columns of its own: it takes the ones time and group name, or else the ones ilm_future() recorded, and with neither, the prediction stops.

Covariates given as draws

A covariate that is not known in advance, such as next month's temperature, can be given as draws from its own forecast. newdata then carries a .draw column: one block of rows per covariate draw, every block listing the same rows in the same order, with only the drawn covariates differing. Parameter draw s uses covariate draw ((s - 1) mod C) + 1 of the C, so the prediction mixes over both. nsim is rounded up to a multiple of C, with a message, so that each covariate draw is used equally often.

The prediction has one row per row of a block. A drawn covariate shows as NA in the rows where it varies, meta records C and the drawn columns, and a drawn row's estimate is its predictive median, as a new unit's is. Intervals conditional on a covariate's point forecast leave out the uncertainty in forecasting it (fpp3, section 10.3). In limn's own study (studies/findings/covariate_draws.md) they covered too little: 0.75 to 0.83 for 90% gaussian intervals, against about 0.90 with the covariate given as draws. ilm_covariate_paths() builds the blocks from an illume model of the covariate, and ilm_as_draws() from paths simulated by another tool.

Uncertainty

  • "joint" (the default): every parameter is drawn jointly, the variances included. In limn's prototype study of few groups (studies/prototypes/), it came closest to nominal coverage for a new unit's observation, though still below it: 0.88 for 90% intervals with 8 groups, against 0.85-0.87 for the other methods it tried, each with a simulation standard error of about 0.01.

  • "fixed": the variance parameters are held at their estimates, and everything else is drawn.

  • "latent": every parameter is held at its estimate, the dispersion included, and only the random effects and the cells of a correlation over time are drawn, from their distribution given the parameters. For a gaussian model with a correlation over time this is a Kalman filter's forecast, which treats the parameters as known; limn's tests check it against stats::KalmanForecast(). ARIMA prediction intervals likewise leave out the variation in the parameter estimates (fpp3, section 9.8).

  • "none": the plug-in prediction at the estimates, with no parameter uncertainty. A new unit's effects, and a series' cells at times it was not fitted at (a forecast, a bridge or a backcast), are still drawn, and covariates given as draws are still mixed over; otherwise a new observation's distribution is the family's alone.

Checks

What each check means and what to do about it, in the words it is printed with. A reference supports what was found and why; a remedy draws on it only where it says so, and anything marked as limn's own reasoning is not the source's:

  • few groups, means (warn): a random term has k levels, fewer than about 20. With so few groups the fit's normal approximation understates the uncertainty in the fixed effects, since it takes no account of the uncertainty in the variances (the reference shows this for linear mixed models), so intervals for means cover as z-intervals do: in limn's coverage study with 8 groups, a 90% interval for a typical unit's mean covered 0.84 to 0.86 for gaussian, Poisson, negative binomial and beta outcomes (binary outcomes covered 0.92). Reference: Kenward and Roger (1997), Biometrics 53, 983-997, pp. 983-984. No remedy for these intervals has been measured yet, so read them as somewhat too narrow; more groups is the sure cure.

  • few groups, new units (warn): a random term has k levels, fewer than about 20. With so few groups the variance between them is poorly determined: the reference found its standard error too small with 50 groups or fewer, for linear models fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. In limn's coverage study with 8 groups, intervals for a new unit's observation covered 0.87 to 0.90 at 90%. Reference: Maas and Hox (2005), Methodology 1, 86-92, pp. 86 and 89-90. Refit with reml = TRUE in illume::ilm_model(): restricted maximum likelihood is almost always at least as good as maximum likelihood, and sometimes better, especially at estimating variances (the reference, p. 89, citing Browne 1998). In limn's prototype study of few groups (studies/prototypes/) it raised 8-group coverage from 0.872 to 0.892 (Poisson) and from 0.891 to 0.903 (gaussian).

  • few groups, new units, REML fit (warn): a random term has k levels, fewer than about 20. With so few groups the variance between them is poorly determined: the reference found its standard error too small with 50 groups or fewer, for linear models fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. In limn's coverage study with 8 groups, intervals for a new unit's observation covered 0.87 to 0.90 at 90%. Reference: Maas and Hox (2005), Methodology 1, 86-92, pp. 86 and 89-90. The fit already used restricted maximum likelihood (REML), the refit this check otherwise suggests. In limn's prototype study of few groups (studies/prototypes/), with REML and 8 groups of 6, 90% intervals for a new unit's observation covered 0.892 (Poisson) and 0.903 (gaussian), with simulation standard errors of 0.004 to 0.005. More groups is the sure cure.

  • unseen levels (note): Some of the rows name a level the fit has not seen. Under groups = "fitted" a unit with no estimated effects can only be predicted as a new one. They are predicted as new units, with effects drawn from the fitted distribution, and marked in the new_level column. If they were meant to be units in the fit, check how their levels are spelt.

  • deterministic trend (warn): The model trends in time (its trend terms). Forecasts past the data assume that the trend's slope does not change (the reference, section 10.4), so their intervals leave out any change in it (limn's own reasoning). A random slope in time gives each unit a trend of its own, and forecasts assume that each unit's slope does not change either (limn's own reasoning). Many smooths continue past the data as a straight line, so a wiggle near the end of the data can drive the forecast (Clark and Wells 2023, Methods in Ecology and Evolution 14, section 1); illume's default smooth does (limn's own measurement). Reference: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021), Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition, section 10.4, with 9.5 ('Understanding ARIMA models') and 9.8 ('Prediction intervals'). A correlation over time can take the trend's place, and each choice is an assumption about the series past the data. If it should return to a level: ar = ilm_ar1(~ time | series), or ilm_car1() for uneven times, or, when the model has one, its own term. Its forecasts go back to zero, so the forecast goes back to the fixed part, and the spread it adds levels off (the reference, section 9.5, 'Understanding ARIMA models', and section 9.8, 'Prediction intervals', for a series; for a latent term, and for ilm_car1(), limn's own reasoning). A trend left in the fixed part still carries the forecast, and its uncertainty still grows. If the level should be free to move: a random walk, ar = ilm_rw1(~ time | series), whose intervals keep widening; at longer horizons it is the safer choice (the reference, section 10.4).

  • boundary draws (fail): Some of the draws of a variance are not finite. Its estimate (SD near zero) is at the edge of its range, where the data cannot resolve it, and the fit did not hold it there. Predict with uncertainty = "fixed", which holds the variances at their estimates, or refit with boundary = "avoid" in illume::ilm_model(), which keeps the variance off the edge with a small penalty.

  • draws not computed (fail): Some of the draws of the mean could not be computed. Averaging over units failed where a draw's variance reaches a large value, as happens when the variance is poorly determined, for instance with few groups. Predict with uncertainty = "fixed", which holds the variances at their estimates.

  • draws not computed (fail): Some of the draws of the mean could not be computed. A draw's value overflowed or was undefined. Predict with uncertainty = "fixed", which holds the variances at their estimates.

  • draws not computed (fail): Some of the draws of a new observation's distribution could not be computed. In those draws the linear predictor or the dispersion ran so far out that the family overflowed. That happens when a parameter sits at the edge of its range (a variance or residual SD near zero, a correlation near 1) and the fit did not hold it there, so its draws spread without limit. Predict with uncertainty = "fixed", which holds the variances at their estimates, or uncertainty = "latent", which holds the dispersion too.

What is not here yet

  • Multinomial outcomes come later, with forecasts of their latent state.

  • Binomial outcomes with more than one trial are predicted per trial.

The prediction object

Read a prediction through as.data.frame() or summary() where you can. Its elements are listed here so that nothing in it is hidden. Every prediction, class "ilm_pred", has:

  • kind: "response" for a new observation's distribution, held as the family's parameters in each draw; "mean" or "link" for draws of the mean or the linear predictor; or "sample" for simulated outcomes, which is how ilm_aggregate() holds some totals.

  • rows: a data frame with one row per predicted row: newdata's columns (one block's, with drawn covariates NA; see Covariates given as draws), and new_level, TRUE where a row names a level the fit has not seen. A total or an average has its by columns and n_rows instead, and an average also weight.

  • weights: the draws' weights, which sum to 1.

  • meta: a list recording how the prediction was made. It has target, groups (one "term = choice" per term), uncertainty, draws (the number of parameter draws), nsim, family, seed, and response, the name of the response column. With covariates given as draws it also has covariate_draws and drawn. Where its time and series columns are known (see Time and series columns), it has time and series, their names.

  • checks: a data frame of the checks the prediction raised (see Checks), one row each, with columns id, check, status, detail, cause, suggestion, reference and values. It has no rows when nothing was found.

  • origin: each row's forecast origin, its series' last observed time, or NA for a row that is not ahead of its series' data.

A prediction straight from ilm_predict() or ilm_forecast() also has new_unit, TRUE where a row's effects are drawn as a new unit's or a new series'. A total or an average has what instead, saying how it was taken, and meta records the same in aggregate.

What else it holds depends on kind:

  • "response": dist, the family's distribution functions as illume::ilm_dist() gives them; lp, a named list of rows-by-draws matrices of linear predictors; par, the family's other parameters in each draw; and pvec, any parameter that is a vector in each draw, such as an ordered outcome's thresholds.

  • "mean" and "link": draws, a rows-by-draws matrix of the predicted values, and estimate, the value at the estimates (a new unit's or a drawn row's predictive median; see Value).

  • "sample": draws, a rows-by-samples matrix of simulated outcomes; estimate, their median; and dist, the family and whether it is discrete.

References

Hyndman, R. J. and Athanasopoulos, G. (2021). Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition. OTexts. Section 9.8, "Forecasting" (ARIMA), and section 10.3, "Forecasting" (dynamic regression) (online edition, https://otexts.com/fpp3/, read 17 October 2026).

See also

ilm_forecast() for forecasts; ilm_aggregate() and ilm_average() for totals and averages over rows; ilm_pit() and ilm_scores.ilm_pred() to check it against outcomes; ilm_plot_fan().

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(site = factor(rep(1:24, each = 5)), x = rnorm(120))
d$y <- rpois(120, exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$x + rnorm(24, 0, 0.5)[d$site]))
fit <- illume::ilm_model(y ~ x + (1 | site), data = d, family = "poisson",
                         verbose = FALSE)
nd <- data.frame(site = c("1", "2", "new"), x = 0)
as.data.frame(ilm_predict(fit, nd, groups = "fitted", nsim = 200))
#>   site x new_level estimate     mean lower_0.9 upper_0.9
#> 1    1 0     FALSE 1.248385 1.309497 0.8112306  2.001837
#> 2    2 0     FALSE 2.091386 2.160922 1.5311525  3.048817
#> 3  new 0      TRUE 1.545643 1.676481 0.8835637  2.972637
as.data.frame(ilm_predict(fit, nd, target = "response", groups = "new",
                          nsim = 200))
#>   site x new_level estimate     mean lower_0.9 upper_0.9
#> 1    1 0     FALSE        1 1.672268         0         4
#> 2    2 0     FALSE        1 1.598920         0         4
#> 3  new 0     FALSE        1 1.659086         0         4
